title: Novel Properties of Hierarchical Probabilistic Partitions and Their Algorithmic Applications
authors: Sandip Banerjee (IDSIA USI-SUPSI, Switzerland), Yair Bartal (The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel), Lee-Ad Gottlieb (Ariel University, Israel), Alon Hovav (The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel)
abstract: We present a refined construction of hierarchical probabilistic partitions with novel properties, substantially stronger than previously known. Our construction provides a family of hierarchical partitions enabling fast dynamic programming algorithms, by guaranteeing that given a sparse set of balls, each cell of the hierarchical partition intersects only a small number of balls. The number of balls intersecting a cell is bounded solely as a function of the padding parameter of the partition (which is bounded in particular by the doubling dimension). This is in contrast to standard guarantees for probabilistic partitions which holds only in expectation. Additionally, each cell of our partition has a significantly smaller description than in previous constructions. These novel partition properties allow faster dynamic programs for a wide spectrum of fundamental problems defined by inherent or implicit sparsity. Among our main applications highlighting the utility of the novel properties are two well-studied clustering problems: min-sum radii (MSR) and min-sum diameters (MSD) clustering. The input to both these problems is a metric space and an integer k, and the goal is to partition the space into k clusters so as to minimize the sum of radii or diameters of the clusters, respectively. We apply our construction to give dramatically improved exact and approximation algorithms for these problems in Euclidean and doubling spaces, planar graphs, and more general settings. In particular, we obtain for these problems the first PTAS for doubling spaces, improving and generalizing upon the time bounds known for Euclidean space, even achieving linear time algorithms for fixed parameter k. We also obtain the first PTAS for MSR for all metrics of bounded padding parameter, including planar and minor excluded metrics. Moreover, our results extend to constrained variants such as fair MSR and mergeable MSR, dramatically improving upon the best known results on these problems in low dimension. Our methods also extend to other clustering problems, including alpha-MSR and alpha-MSD (where the measure is the sum of radii or diameters raised to power of alpha), as well as aversion clustering, providing in similar settings the first QPTAS and first fixed parameter PTAS for these problems. Moreover, many of our clustering results extend to the corresponding clustering problems with outliers. Our construction applies as well to a wide range of network design problems possessing inherent sparsity properties in doubling spaces. Notably, we can apply our method to dramatically improve upon the best known bounds for the traveling salesman (TSP) and Steiner tree problems in doubling spaces. Similarly, we significantly improve upon the best known run-times for Steiner forest, TSP with neighborhoods, prize collecting TSP, and 2-ECSS (two edge-connected spanning subgraph), all in doubling spaces. Our new constructions of hierarchical probabilistic partitions present a major simplification of previous methods, and provide a more natural and useful tool for future applications.

Abstract
We present a refined construction of hierarchical probabilistic partitions with novel properties, substantially
stronger than previously known. Our construction provides a family of hierarchical partitions enabling fast dynamic
programming algorithms, by guaranteeing that given a sparse set of balls, each cell of the hierarchical partition
intersects only a small number of balls. The number of balls intersecting a cell is bounded solely as a function of the
padding parameter of the partition (which is bounded in particular by the doubling dimension). This is in contrast to
standard guarantees for probabilistic partitions which holds only in expectation. Additionally, each cell of our partition
has a significantly smaller description than in previous constructions. These novel partition properties allow faster
dynamic programs for a wide spectrum of fundamental problems defined by inherent or implicit sparsity.
Among our main applications highlighting the utility of the novel properties are two well-studied clustering
problems: min-sum radii (MSR) and min-sum diameters (MSD) clustering. The input to both these problems is a
metric space and an integer k, and the goal is to partition the space into k clusters so as to minimize the sum of
radii or diameters of the clusters, respectively. We apply our construction to give dramatically improved exact and
approximation algorithms for these problems in Euclidean and doubling spaces, planar graphs, and more general
settings. In particular, we obtain for these problems the first PTAS for doubling spaces, improving and generalizing
upon the time bounds known for Euclidean space, even achieving linear time algorithms for fixed parameter k. We
also obtain the first PTAS for MSR for all metrics of bounded padding parameter, including planar and minor excluded
metrics. Moreover, our results extend to constrained variants such as fair MSR and mergeable MSR, dramatically
improving upon the best known results on these problems in low dimension.
Our methods also extend to other clustering problems, including α-MSR and α-MSD (where the measure is the
sum of radii or diameters raised to power of α), as well as aversion clustering, providing in similar settings the first
QPTAS and first fixed parameter PTAS for these problems. Moreover, many of our clustering results extend to the
corresponding clustering problems with outliers.
Our construction applies as well to a wide range of network design problems possessing inherent sparsity properties
in doubling spaces. Notably, we can apply our method to dramatically improve upon the best known bounds for the
traveling salesman (TSP) and Steiner tree problems in doubling spaces. Similarly, we significantly improve upon
the best known run-times for Steiner forest, TSP with neighborhoods, prize collecting TSP, and 2-ECSS (two
edge-connected spanning subgraph), all in doubling spaces.
Our new constructions of hierarchical probabilistic partitions present a major simplification of previous methods,
and provide a more natural and useful tool for future applications.

I. I NTRODUCTION

a) Historical perspective:: Arora’s Euclidean traveling
salesman algorithm [Aro98] is a well-known example
of running a dynamic program on top of a hierarchical
partition designed for the Euclidean space. This seminal approach builds a simple hierarchical partition –
specifically, a randomly shifted quad-tree – on top of the
space, and then uses a dynamic program to iteratively
compute the best tours within each respective cell. For
any given cell, its best candidate tours are computed
by combining the best candidate tours of its children.
Importantly, the run-time of the dynamic program features
an exponential dependence on the edge complexity, that
is the maximum number of edges of the target tour cut by
a cell. Specifically for the case of Euclidean spaces, the
Patching Lemma demonstrates that the edge complexity
may be taken as a function of the dimension alone,
independent of the size of the point set. This results
in a Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS),
an approximation algorithm characterized by polynomial
run-time for any fixed approximation factor (1 + ).

Metric partitions are a basic tool in the field of metric
embeddings, and they find broad algorithmic application
for problems in the fields of clustering, network design,
and the like. A partition P of a metric space (X, d)
is a collection of pairwise disjoint subsets C(P ) =
{C1 , C2 , . . . , Ct } satisfying that X = ∪j Cj . The sets
Cj ∈ C(P ) are called clusters (or cells), and the clusters
are bounded if their is an upper-bound on their diameters.
A probabilistic partition is a distribution over a set of
partitions for the metric (X, d). These are particularly
important and widely-used, constituting a central tool in
the theory of metric embedding and its applications. They
possess the useful property that every fixed ball or point
pair (also referred to as an edge) in the underlying space
is cut with some small probability – where a set is said
to be cut by a partition if its points do not all fall in the
same partition cluster. This property is in turn described
by the padding parameter τ of the partition; this is an
upper-bound on the ratio between the probability that
any given ball or edge is cut by the partition and the
diameter of that ball or edge. Probabilistic partitions were
introduced and first constructed for general n-point metric
spaces by [Bar96] with a tight bound of τ = O(log n).
A more refined bound of τ = O(d) can be provided
[GKL03], [ABN11], where here d = ddim(X) stands
for the doubling dimension of the space. Probabilistic
partitions were subsequently derived for a wide range
of specific metric spaces, including τ = O(h) for those
defined by a graph with bounded treewidth h or excluded
minor Kh [AGG+ 14] (and so τ = O(1) for planar
metrics), and τ = O(log g) for graphs with genus g.

Arora’s algorithmic approach can be extended, for example, to metric spaces with bounded doubling dimension. But in this and other more general settings, wellstructured hierarchies such as the quad-tree do not exist,
and subsequently the Patching Lemma does not hold.
Instead, Talwar [Tal04] constructed a hierarchical probabilistic partition by intersecting a series of probabilistic
partitions for doubling spaces [GKL03], [ABN11], where
each subsequent partition (or level) has a diameter bound
half that of the previous level. (For TSP and many other
problems, the aspect ratio of the space can be bounded
as poly(n) [Aro98], so the number of partitions in the
series is O(log n).) This means that the space is iteratively
partitioned into cells of progressively smaller diameter
bound. This approach yields cells of polylogarithmic edge
complexity: A single cell is formed by the intersection
O(log n) partitions, and each one can cut multiple edges
of the optimal tour. As the dynamic program runs in time
exponential in the edge complexity, this results in a QuasiPolynomial Time Approximation Scheme (QPTAS). 1

A hierarchical probabilistic partition is constructed by
superimposing a series of probabilistic partitions with
clusters of increasingly smaller diameters, with each
probabilistic partition maintaining its padding property.
This technique yields a nested partition of the space
into progressively smaller cells. This is central to many
algorithmic constructions and numerous applications,
most notably in the construction of probabilistic embeddings into hierarchically separated trees (HST) [Bar96],
metric embeddings [ABN11], [BFN22], and a large range
of approximation algorithms (e.g. [Aro98], [BGK16],
[GKK+ 10]). For the case of approximation algorithms,
a dynamic program is typically run on top of the
hierarchical partition, to compute an exact or approximate
answer to the underlying problem. It is therefore inherent
that hierarchical partitions serve as a basic building block
in designing efficient approximation algorithms.

spaces was addressed in [BGK16]. They first showed that
in this setting, the traveling salesman problem can be
decomposed into smaller sub-instances, and the solution
tours of the sub-instances joined into a single approximate

c) Our contribution: A new hierarchical family.: Let us
first generalize the above notion of sparsity from edges to
balls: Define a λ-sparse set of balls B to be one for which
the sum of radii of balls of B residing within any larger
ball of radius r (the latter ball not necessarily in B) is at
most λr (see Definition 1). This definition broadens the
class of sparse problems to also include many clustering
problems, as we show below. A desired goal for achieving
fast dynamic programming algorithms for these problems
is a hierarchical partition with small ball complexity
(a generalization of edge complexity) defined as the
maximum number of balls cut by a hierarchical cell.
A reduction in level complexity is similarly desirable.
For problems admitting λ-sparse solutions, we introduce
a new family of hierarchical partitions, sufficiently robust
as to apply to all spaces admitting bounded probabilistic
partitions with padding parameter τ . We demonstrate that
this family exhibits dramatically better properties than
those used in [BGK16], and includes some hierarchical
partitions with ball complexity only O(λτ log(λτ )). This
is the first such bound independent of n, dramatically
better than the previous bound of O(λτ log(min{Φ, n}))
used by [Tal04], [GKK+ 10] (where Φ is the aspect ratio
of the space). At the same time, these same partitions have
the property√that each cell is formed by the intersection
of only O( log n) levels (i.e. its level complexity).

In attempting to run an efficient dynamic program upon
the above family, [BGK16] encountered an additional
problem: The dynamic program must consider each cell
in the entire family. Yet for any given point, its containing
cell at some level may be formed by the intersection of
probabilistic hierarchies at all higher levels – the number
of these forming levels is the level complexity of the
cell. The number of different cells throughout the whole
family that can contain the point is approximately the
number of candidate probabilistic partitions raised to the
level complexity, and this is again super-polynomial. To
overcome this challenge, the hierarchical construction in
[BGK16] reduced the number of levels in the construction
to O(log n/ log log n) by having the diameters decrease
by a factor of logΘd (1) n instead of by a constant factor.
This decreased the level complexity, at the cost of
increasing the number of child cells per parent cell,
which implied an increase in the number of possible
partition configurations. The ultimate run-time achieved

Further innovative ideas are necessary for individual applications of our hierarchical partition family construction
and their analyses, as described below.

d) Innovation.: Structurally, our family is constructed in
a top-down fashion similar to the approach adopted by
[BGK16]. One important structural difference, both for
improving the run-time and for generalizing to all spaces
admitting bounded probabilistic partitions, is that instead
of sampling candidate partitions for each individual cell,
we pre-sample a set of only O(log n) candidate partitions
for each level, meaning for the partitioning of all cells
in that level for all hierarchies in the family. A second
important difference is that our improved bounds and
analysis allow a construction with the full O(log n)
hierarchical levels, meaning that the partition diameters
are reduced by only a constant in each level.

e) Applications.: To highlight the applicability of our
new hierarchies, we revisit and explore two basic and
well-studied clustering problems: min-sum radii (MSR)
and min-sum diameters (MSD) clustering. For these
problems, the input is a set of metric points along with an
integral parameter k, and the goal is to produce k clusters,
while minimizing the sum of cluster radii or diameters,
respectively, where for MSR the clusters are defined
by balls.3 It is easy to see that these problems possess
inherent sparsity, since a solution with a sufficiently dense
concentration of balls in some area can be improved by
replacing these balls with a single ball covering all their
points, at lower cost. It follows that our hierarchical
partitions can be applied to these clustering problems.
The application is however non-trivial: Applying our hierarchical partitions requires deriving bounds on the number
of balls that can be in the proximity of a cell. Further,
an efficient execution of the dynamic program requires
limiting the number of candidate solution clusters, which
in turn necessitates an intricate analysis exploiting the
properties of the probabilistic hierarchical partition, and
allows the solution cost to increase upon small probability
events of solution clusters being cut.

Our central contribution is in the improved bounds and
analysis alluded to above, which yield low level and
ball complexities: We show that there exist hierarchical
partitions within the above family with low level complexity. All cells of these
√ hierarchies are formed by the
intersections of only O( log n) levels, with the majority
of levels not impacting the points found in the cell. We
show that this holds for any given cell with sufficiently
high probability so that it may hold simultaneously for
all cells of a hierarchy.
Our most intriguing and challenging contribution is the
proof that the ball complexity is dependent solely on the
sparsity and padding parameter. Here we make use of
the assumed underlying sparsity of the solution. While
standard analysis can show that this property holds for
each cell in expectation, proving that it can hold for
all cells simultaneously is far more challenging. This
requires the definition of substantial formation, which
addresses a situation in which a cell, formed by the
intersection of higher level partitions, cuts a proximate
solution ball. Informally, we say that a higher level
partition substantially forms the cell if there is such a
solution ball that is cut by this partition. We achieve the
desired bound by showing that with high probability a
cell can’t be substantially formed by more than bounded
number of high level partitions.
